title: Fault tolerance: how systems fail
problem: Redundant copies that share a rack, a dependency or a deploy fail together, and a server that passes its health check while dropping packets keeps receiving traffic.
summary: Faults become errors become failures, and tolerance means breaking that chain. Spread copies across failure domains they do not share, pick a redundancy shape for the failure you expect, keep the blast radius small, and detect the grey failures that health checks miss.
catTip: Two naps in the same sunbeam are not redundancy. When the cloud rolls in, both naps fail at once. I keep a spare nap spot by the radiator in a different room, and I test it on Tuesdays.

recall.q: What is a failure domain, and how should redundancy relate to it?
recall.a: A failure domain is a set of things that fail together: a host, a rack, an availability zone, a region, or everything behind one deploy. Redundant copies only protect against failures of domains they do not share, so place them across the domain you want to survive.

guide.breaks: Two replicas in one rack die together when the switch fails, one config service takes down both regions, and a host that answers health checks while timing out real requests keeps getting traffic.
guide.tradeoffs: Every failure domain you span adds latency, replication lag or cost, active-active copies need headroom to absorb a lost peer, and catching grey failure means measuring from the caller's side instead of trusting a health check.
guide.explainSimply: Things break in layers: a flaw turns into a wrong state, which turns into something a user notices. Keeping spare copies only helps if the copies cannot break for the same reason, like keeping a spare house key with a neighbour instead of on the same keyring. Some breakages are sneaky: the server says it is fine while quietly doing a terrible job.
guide.hint: Ask what the copies have in common: the rack, the zone, the dependency, the deploy.

meow: Two meows on one keyring. Lose the ring, lose both. Spare meow lives next door.

quiz.prompt: A service runs two replicas on two hosts in the same rack, behind a load balancer. Which event does this redundancy not protect against?
options: One process is killed for running out of memory
One host is rebooted for a kernel patch
quiz.explanation: Both hosts share the rack's switch and power, so a rack-level fault takes both replicas at once: redundancy only covers failure domains the copies do not share. The other three are single-host faults that the second replica absorbs.

quiz.prompt: What makes a grey failure hard to detect?
options: The process crashes so quickly that no log line is written
The component passes the health checks the system relies on while callers see errors or slowness
It only affects the passive standby, which receives no traffic
It corrupts the metrics pipeline so no alerts can fire
quiz.explanation: Grey failure is defined by differential observability: the failure detector sees a healthy component while applications see a failing one, so the fix is to measure from the caller's side. A fast crash is the easy case, since the health check fails and the process is replaced.

cards.q: A disk sector goes bad, the database returns a corrupted row, and the app shows a blank page. Label the fault, the error and the failure, and say why the chain matters.
cards.a: Fault: the bad sector. Error: the corrupted row in the database's state. Failure: the blank page the user sees (the database's failure was itself a fault for the app). Fault tolerance means breaking the chain at some link, for example a checksum that catches the error before it becomes a failure.

cards.q: A primary runs in zone A with a hot standby in zone B, and both load their configuration from one config service in zone A. What is wrong?
cards.a: The config service is a shared dependency, so a zone-A outage takes down both copies: a correlated failure. Redundancy needs the copies to share nothing in the domain you want to survive, so the config must be cached locally or served from both zones.

glossary.note: One or more data centres with independent power, cooling and networking inside a cloud region; replicas spread across AZs survive the loss of a data centre.

sources.title: Avižienis, Laprie, Randell, Landwehr, "Basic Concepts and Taxonomy of Dependable and Secure Computing", IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing 1(1), 2004
sources.supports: the fault, error, failure vocabulary and the chain in which a component's failure is a fault for the system containing it

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Dependability" (fault, error, failure chain)
sources.supports: the fault-error-failure chain and the four means (prevention, tolerance, removal, forecasting), read as coverage of the taxonomy paper

sources.title: Lamport, Shostak, Pease, "The Byzantine Generals Problem", ACM TOPLAS 4(3), 1982
sources.supports: the origin and naming of Byzantine faults; bibliographic details confirmed via Wikipedia's 'Byzantine fault' article

sources.title: AWS whitepaper, "AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries: Availability Zones"
sources.supports: an AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, networking and connectivity; zones up to 60 miles (about 100 km) apart, close enough for synchronous replication; generators and cooling not shared; AWS deployments to zones in one region are separated in time

sources.title: Huang et al., "Gray Failure: The Achilles' Heel of Cloud-Scale Systems", HotOS 2017
sources.supports: the term grey failure, the HotOS 2017 venue, and differential observability as its key feature (the publication page lists the first author as Ryan Huang)

sources.title: Amazon Builders' Library, "Implementing health checks"
sources.supports: liveness, local and dependency health checks; correlated false positives from dependency checks; fail-open load balancers; anomaly detection by comparing a server with its peers

sources.title: AWS Well-Architected guidance, "Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture: What is a cell-based architecture?"
sources.supports: a failure in one of ten cells leaves 90% of requests unaffected; fault-isolation boundaries limit the scope of impact of bad deployments and poison-pill requests

sources.title: Google SRE Book, ch. 22 "Addressing Cascading Failures"
sources.supports: the N+2 provisioning example (six clusters for a 19,000 QPS peak when each breaks at 5,000 QPS)

sources.title: AWS whitepaper, "Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS: Disaster recovery options in the cloud"
sources.supports: active/passive versus active/active definitions (the passive site serves no traffic until failover)
